title: Patterns in Mathematics — Chapter Summary
intro: Mathematics is the search for patterns. A pattern is an arrangement of numbers, shapes or objects that follows a rule. Once you spot the rule, you can predict what comes next, count without listing every item, and explain WHY things behave as they do. This chapter trains your eye to spot patterns — first in numbers, then in shapes — and to express the rules behind them.

branches.label: Shape patterns
details: Each shape generates a number sequence

sections.heading: What is Mathematics?
bullets: Mathematics is the study of patterns and relationships, not just arithmetic.
Mathematicians ask: 'What comes next?', 'Why does this rule work?', 'Can we describe it with a formula?'
The power of mathematics: spot a pattern, explain it, apply it to many situations.

sections.heading: Patterns in Numbers
bullets: A number sequence is a list of numbers that follow a rule.
Counting numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, … (add 1).
Even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8, … (add 2).  Odd: 1, 3, 5, 7, …
Square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, … (n × n).
Triangular numbers: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, … (1 + 2 + … + n).
Cube numbers: 1, 8, 27, 64, … (n × n × n).
Powers of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … (double).  Powers of 3: 1, 3, 9, 27, …
Fibonacci: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … (sum of previous two).

sections.heading: Visualising Number Sequences
bullets: Many number sequences become CLEARER when we draw them.
Counting numbers: dots in a row.
Square numbers: a square grid of dots — n × n.
Triangular numbers: a triangle of dots — 1 dot in row 1, 2 in row 2, 3 in row 3, …
Drawing helps us spot the rule and prove WHY a formula works.

sections.heading: Relations Among Sequences
bullets: Sum of first n odd numbers = n^2: 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n^2.
Triangular(n) = n × (n + 1) / 2.
Two consecutive triangular numbers add to a square: triangular(n) + triangular(n + 1) = (n + 1)^2.
Each rule has a picture-proof using dots — drawing makes the WHY obvious.
Use the formula for fast computation: 1 + 2 + … + 100 = 5050 (no need to add term-by-term).

sections.heading: Patterns in Shapes
bullets: A line of n squares matches the n-th counting number.
A staircase of n rows (1, 2, 3, …, n squares per row) matches the n-th triangular number.
An n × n grid of squares matches the n-th square number.
Pentagonal arrangements give 1, 5, 12, 22, 35 …
Every neat shape sequence has a number rule, and every neat number sequence has a shape.

sections.heading: Connecting Number and Shape Patterns
bullets: Number patterns and shape patterns are TWO views of the same idea.
When the rule isn't obvious from the numbers, draw the shape.
When the rule isn't obvious from the shape, write down the numbers.
Switching between views is a powerful problem-solving habit.
Mathematics is the search for patterns — once you see one, the world looks different.

key_takeaways: Mathematics is the study of patterns and relationships.
A number sequence follows a rule; identify it to find the next term.
Square (n × n), triangular (n(n+1)/2), and cube (n × n × n) are the most useful.
Sum of first n odd numbers = n^2 — useful and beautiful.
Drawing dot patterns helps reveal hidden rules.
Number patterns and shape patterns are two views of the same idea — switch between them when stuck.

glossary.definition: An arrangement of numbers, shapes or objects that follows a rule.
A list of numbers in a particular order, generated by a rule.
A whole number not divisible by 2 (1, 3, 5, …).
A number that is the product of a counting number with itself: 1, 4, 9, 16, …
A number obtained by 1 + 2 + … + n; the sequence is 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, …
A number that is n × n × n for some counting number n: 1, 8, 27, 64, …
The sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, … in which each term is the sum of the two preceding terms.
The pattern by which each term is obtained from the previous ones.
